explanations.explanation: That's what the text says: when Ish-bosheth heard Abner had died in Hebron, "…he lost courage…" Abner was the army commander who had put him on the throne (2 Samuel 2:8-9), so I think the news hit him hard. Picture the one holding your whole plan together suddenly gone. Nobody's knees stay steady after that.

I can see why you'd pick it, since a king usually rallies his soldiers. But the text never has Ish-bosheth do that. It says he lost courage. His first move isn't a battle plan, it's a sinking feeling.

That would be a big move, but the text doesn't have Ish-bosheth send anything to David, the king over Judah (2 Samuel 2:4). What it says is that he heard the news and lost courage. The only message that reaches David in this chapter comes from two other men, and we'll get to them.

Close, but the text says more than that. Yes, Ish-bosheth lost courage, but it adds that "…all Israel was dismayed." So the whole nation felt the news about Abner, not just the king. When the biggest name in the room is gone, everybody feels it.
That's right, baker. The text says Ish-bosheth "…lost courage, and all Israel was dismayed." So he had company. The whole nation was dismayed too.
Yes, they are "…of the tribe of Benjamin…" The text says Beeroth is considered part of Benjamin. Their father Rimmon is called a Beerothite. A name and a tribe, all packed in one verse.

Judah is a fair guess, since David was anointed king over Judah (2 Samuel 2:4) and the story is heading to his door. But these two brothers serve Ish-bosheth, Saul's son. The text puts them in the tribe of Benjamin, and says Beeroth is considered part of Benjamin.

Ephraim is a real tribe of Israel (Joshua 16:5), but it isn't the one named here. The text says Baanah and Rechab are from the tribe of Benjamin. It even explains that Beeroth counts as part of Benjamin.

That's it. His nurse picked him up and ran, but "…as she was hurrying to escape, he fell and became lame." He was five years old, and the text says he was lame in his feet. It's a sad little detail to find in the middle of this chapter.

explanations.answer: He is captured on the road
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anyone captured him. His nurse picked him up and fled. In the hurry, he fell and became lame. That fall is the part of the story the text tells us.

explanations.answer: He is left behind in Jezreel
explanations.explanation: The text says the report about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel, but it doesn't say the boy was left there. His nurse picked him up and fled. He fell as she hurried to escape.
Yes, his name was Mephibosheth. The text introduces him quickly here, just as the boy who fell. Hang on to the name, because David speaks to him later (2 Samuel 9:6).
Asahel is a name from earlier in 2 Samuel. He was Joab's brother (2 Samuel 2:18). The boy who fell is not him. The text names Jonathan's son Mephibosheth.

Ahimaaz is a real name in the book of Samuel (2 Samuel 15:27), but it's not the one given for this boy. The text says Jonathan's son, the one who fell, was named Mephibosheth. Easy to mix up when the names run long, baker.

Right, it was a midday nap. The text says Rechab and Baanah came in the heat of the day, "…while the king was taking his midday nap." This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it's a hard one to read.
A walk would put the king up and moving. The text says he was taking his midday nap. They came in the heat of the day, when he was lying down.
The text doesn't send Ish-bosheth to a bath. It says he was taking his midday nap, and verse 7 adds that he was lying on his bed. The heat of the day was when they chose to come.
That's the cover story. They entered the interior of the house "…as if to get some wheat…" It's a plain, ordinary errand. The text says that's how it looked, and then they stabbed him in the stomach.
A report would at least sound official, but that's not what the text says. They walked in "…as if to get some wheat…" Nothing in the verse has them carrying news to the king.

Guarding sounds like a job for two men who lead raiding parties, but the text doesn't use it. They went in "…as if to get some wheat…" What they really did inside was stab the king, so the errand was only a show.
Yes. The text says they "…traveled all night by way of the Arabah." Their destination was David at Hebron. They went all night with no stops mentioned, carrying what they had taken from the king.
The text says it's true. Rechab and Baanah "…traveled all night by way of the Arabah." Then they brought Ish-bosheth's head to David at Hebron. A whole night on the road, and the text gives no stops.
Yes, they brought it "…to David at Hebron…" That's where David was anointed king over Judah (2 Samuel 2:4), and it's where Abner died. A lot of this story keeps coming back to one city.
Gath is a different city from the one in the text. The brothers brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron. That's the name to hold onto, since the chapter ends there too.
Gibeah isn't where they went. The text says they brought the head of Ish-bosheth "…to David at Hebron…" Hebron is where the brothers meet the king they came to see.

explanations.answer: Granted him vengeance on Saul's family
explanations.explanation: That's what they claim. They say, "Today the LORD has granted vengeance to my lord the king against Saul and his offspring." They say the LORD did this for David. David's answer, though, shows he doesn't take it that way.

explanations.answer: Paid him back for Abner's death
explanations.explanation: Abner's death is in the background, but it's not what they say. Their words are that the LORD "…has granted vengeance to my lord the king against Saul and his offspring." They talk about Saul's family, not Abner. And Abner, as we saw, got buried in a tomb in Hebron.

explanations.answer: Given him peace with all of Israel
explanations.explanation: Peace sounds nice, but it's not what the two brothers say. They claim the LORD has granted vengeance "…against Saul and his offspring." Their whole speech is about Saul's family, and nothing about peace in it.
David points to that man as a warning, not a model. He says he seized him and put him to death at Ziklag. Then he says, "That was his reward for his news!" No gift involved, baker.
Yes, False. David says someone told him "Look, Saul is dead…" and thought he was bringing good news. David seized him and put him to death at Ziklag. That was his reward, in David's words.

That's the word David uses. He says wicked men killed "…a righteous man in his own house and on his own bed…" He calls what they did wicked and he calls Ish-bosheth righteous. Those are David's words, and he says them to the two men standing in front of him.
Foolish isn't David's word. He says "…wicked men kill a righteous man…" The wicked ones are Rechab and Baanah, and Ish-bosheth is the righteous man.
David doesn't use guilty for the man in the bed. He says "…wicked men kill a righteous man in his own house and on his own bed…" The wicked men are the two standing in front of him.

explanations.answer: Bury it in Abner's tomb in Hebron
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. David's young men "…took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in Abner’s tomb in Hebron." Abner was the commander who made Ish-bosheth king (2 Samuel 2:8-9), so the two ended up together. I think that's a quiet, careful ending to a hard scene.

explanations.answer: Return it to Mahanaim for burial
explanations.explanation: Mahanaim is where Abner made Ish-bosheth king (2 Samuel 2:8-9), so it's a fair guess. But the text says they buried the head in Hebron, not in Mahanaim. They didn't carry it anywhere else.
Saul was Ish-bosheth's father, so I see why that came to mind. But the text names a different tomb. David's young men buried the head "…in Abner’s tomb in Hebron."
